**A Thousand Words**

The first thing that comes is the question of what comes first. That's the trap of an open invitation: handed a blank field, the mind immediately starts fencing it. A thousand words, no subject, no constraint—and instantly I'm thinking about constraints, the way a person told to relax becomes a catalogue of their own tensions.

So let me start somewhere small. A kitchen, early morning, before anyone else is awake. There is a particular quality to that hour that everyone knows and no one has fully described: the light hasn't committed yet, the refrigerator hums like it's keeping a secret, and the day exists only as potential. You can stand there with a cup of something warm and feel that you are briefly outside of time—not free of it, exactly, but parked on its shoulder, hazards blinking.

I think about that hour a lot, because it's where most honest thoughts happen. Not the performed thoughts, the ones we rehearse for other people, but the strays. The realization that you've been angry at someone for a year over something they don't remember. The sudden certainty that you should call your mother. The grocery list that interrupts your grief, and the grief that interrupts your grocery list, and the way both of these are equally part of being a person.

We are taught that meaning lives in big things—weddings, funerals, the speech at the end of the movie. But meaning is mostly a sediment. It settles out of ordinary water. The friend who always texts when your flight lands. The neighbor who shovels two extra feet of sidewalk past their property line. The way someone learned how you take your coffee and never made a ceremony of knowing it. Nobody writes epics about this material, which is strange, because it's the material everyone is actually made of.

Here is something else that comes: an old man I once read about who spent forty years recording the date the ice broke up on the lake near his house. Just that. One date per year, in a notebook. He wasn't a scientist. He had no theory. But when climate researchers came looking for long-term data, his notebook turned out to be one of the most valuable records in the region. Forty years of paying attention to one thing, faithfully, without knowing why it mattered.

I find that story almost unbearably moving, and I think it's because it suggests a possibility most of us secretly hope for: that attention itself is a form of love, and that love, practiced steadily enough, becomes useful in ways we cannot foresee. The man wasn't trying to save the world. He was just looking at his lake. But looking, it turns out, is not nothing. Looking might be most of it.

The opposite of looking is not blindness. It's hurry. I am suspicious of hurry, even though I live inside it like everyone else. Hurry tells you that the present moment is merely a corridor to a better one, that real life is always one task away. But the corridor is the house. There is no room you finally reach. The man with the lake understood this, or maybe he didn't understand anything and just liked his lake, which amounts to the same wisdom worn casually.

What else comes? Doubt comes. The suspicion that writing about attention is easier than paying it. That essays like this one are a kind of moral window-shopping—admiring the virtues from the sidewalk, hands in pockets, buying nothing. Fair enough. I'll let the doubt stand here in the middle of the piece like a guest who wasn't invited but is making good points.

And then, because the mind is a creature that startles easily and runs in any direction, what comes next is octopuses. An octopus has neurons distributed throughout its arms; in a real sense, its arms think. An octopus reaching into a crevice is not commanding a tool—it is sending a portion of its mind into the dark to find out what's there. I think about this when I think about writing, which is also a way of sending part of the mind into the dark to find out what's there. You don't know what you think until the arm comes back holding something. Sometimes it's a crab. Sometimes it's a bottle cap. You write a thousand words to discover which.

Toward the end of an open field, you start to feel the far fence. So let me say the thing plainly, the thing all the strays seem to circle: most of a life is unwitnessed. The early kitchens, the ice dates, the shoveled sidewalks, the texts when the flight lands. Nobody is keeping the master record. There is no notebook for most of it. And the temptation is to conclude that the unwitnessed parts don't count, that only what's seen and shared and measured is real.

But I think it's the reverse. The unwitnessed parts are the load-bearing walls. They hold everything else up precisely because no one is watching, because they're done for nothing—no credit, no audience, no algorithm. The man wrote down the ice date whether or not anyone would ever read it. For forty years, that was a private act. Then one day it mattered enormously. But here's the thing: it mattered before that, too. It mattered the whole time, the way the kitchen hour matters, the way attention matters—quietly, cumulatively, in the sediment.

So: a thousand words, and what came was a kitchen, a lake, an octopus, and a fence at the far end of a field. Not a thesis so much as a walk. But maybe that's the honest answer to "write whatever comes." What comes is never one thing. What comes is the mind doing what it does in the unwatched hours—wandering, doubting, circling back, reaching its arms into the dark.

And then the light commits. The house wakes up. The day stops being potential and starts being itself. You finish the warm thing in the cup, rinse it, set it upside down on the rack.

The ice, somewhere, is getting ready to break.
